lesson.title: Five Around One: Why PCl5 Breaks the Octet Rule
lesson.summary: Trigonal bipyramidal geometry appears when a central atom, freed by an expanded octet, surrounds itself with five electron domains split between two distinct positions, axial and equatorial, each carrying its own bond angle.
lesson.body:
A steric number of five is where VSEPR theory starts requiring something extra: an expanded octet on the central atom. Five electron domains mean ten electrons surrounding the central atom, two more than the standard octet allows, and only elements from period three and beyond are large enough, with accessible orbitals of the right energy, to accommodate that many domains comfortably. This is why trigonal bipyramidal geometry, unlike linear, trigonal planar, or tetrahedral geometry, only shows up for heavier main group elements such as phosphorus, sulfur, and the halogens beyond period two.

The trigonal bipyramidal shape itself is genuinely different from the shapes covered so far, because it is the first one where all the positions are not geometrically equivalent. Two of the five domains sit in axial positions, pointing directly opposite each other above and below a central plane, 180 degrees apart from one another. The other three domains sit in equatorial positions, spread evenly around that central plane, 120 degrees apart from each other. Between an axial domain and any equatorial domain, the angle is 90 degrees. This split into two different kinds of positions, axial and equatorial, has no earlier parallel in linear, trigonal planar, or tetrahedral geometry, all of which had only one type of position to fill.

Phosphorus pentachloride, PCl5, is the clearest real example of this shape with no lone pairs complicating the picture. Phosphorus, a period three element, forms five single bonds to five chlorine atoms, using all five available bonding domains and leaving no lone pairs behind. With a steric number of five and zero lone pairs, both the electron geometry and the molecular geometry are trigonal bipyramidal. The molecule displays all three of the characteristic bond angles at once: 90 degrees between axial and equatorial chlorines, 120 degrees between neighboring equatorial chlorines, and 180 degrees between the two axial chlorines directly across from each other.

The expanded octet that makes this shape possible is the same concept that governs whether any given central atom is even capable of reaching a steric number of five in the first place. Nitrogen, sitting directly above phosphorus in the periodic table, cannot form an analogous NCl5 molecule, because nitrogen has no low energy orbitals available to expand beyond eight electrons. Phosphorus can, which is exactly why PCl5 exists as a stable, well characterized compound while its nitrogen counterpart does not.

Trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry also serves as the starting framework for several other molecular shapes once lone pairs are introduced in place of one or more bonding domains, since a lone pair will always prefer to occupy an equatorial position rather than an axial one, minimizing its repulsion with the other domains. Those lone pair variations produce shapes with their own separate names, but the base geometry, five domains, two axial and three equatorial, 90, 120, and 180 degree angles, is the essential starting point for understanding any molecule built around a central atom with five electron domains.
